name: ECG 4 · Conduction and chambers
blurb: Grade heart blocks, read bundle blocks, WPW, hypertrophy and pacing.

topics.name: AV blocks
topics.desc: Read the P-to-QRS relationship and grade the block.

cards.q: AV blocks are graded by looking at
cards.a:
How each P wave relates to the QRS

An AV block is a problem getting the atrial impulse to the ventricles, so the P–QRS link is what you read.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.182–184; Khan ch11 p.258

cards.q: Explain: First degree: PR over 0.20 s
cards.a: In first-degree AV block the PR interval is longer than 0.20 s and constant, but every P wave is still followed by a QRS. It is a delay rather than a block, and by itself needs no treatment.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.184–185; Khan ch11 p.258

cards.q: Explain: Mobitz I: the PR stretches, then drops
cards.a: In Mobitz I (Wenckebach) the PR lengthens beat by beat until one P wave is not conducted and a QRS is dropped. The PR after the drop is short again, and the cycle repeats.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.186; Khan ch11 p.259

cards.q: In Wenckebach, the RR interval that contains the dropped P wave is
cards.a:
Shorter than two PP intervals

Khan: the RR containing the blocked P is shorter than the sum of two PP intervals.
cards.note: Khan ch11 p.259

cards.q: Where does Mobitz I block almost always sit?
cards.a:
In the AV node

Wenckebach is a progressive nodal delay, which is why it is usually benign.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.186–189

cards.q: Explain: Mobitz II: fixed PR, sudden drop
cards.a: In Mobitz II the PR stays constant: at least two beats conduct with the same PR, then a P wave suddenly fails to conduct. There is no warning lengthening.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.186–187; Khan ch11 p.259–261

cards.q:
Mobitz II can progress suddenly to complete heart block.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Its block sits below the node and can fail without warning, which is why it needs a pacemaker.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.186–189; Khan ch11 p.261

cards.q: Explain: 2:1 block cannot be typed
cards.a: When every second P wave is dropped, there is only one PR before each drop, so you cannot see whether it lengthens. Call it simply 2:1 AV block, not Mobitz I or II.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.188

cards.q: Explain: Third degree: atria and ventricles part
cards.a: In third-degree (complete) block no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles. P waves march at their own rate and QRS complexes at a slower escape rate, with no link between them: AV dissociation.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.190–191; Khan ch11 p.261–262

cards.q: Complete heart block with a wide QRS at 35/min. The escape focus is
cards.a:
The ventricles

A slow, wide escape arises below the bundle branches, in the ventricle itself.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.190–192; Khan ch11 p.261–262

topics.name: Bundle branch block
topics.desc: Spot RBBB and LBBB from the QRS width and V1.

cards.q: Complete bundle branch block widens the QRS to at least
cards.a:
0.12 s

Both books require a QRS of 0.12 s or more for complete bundle branch block.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.196–198; Khan ch4 p.87

cards.q: Name the leads with the rSR′
cards.a:
V1, V2

V1 and V2 sit over the right ventricle, which fires last and writes the R′.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.197; Khan ch4 p.87–88

cards.q: In RBBB, a wide slurred S wave appears in
cards.a:
I, V5 and V6

The late rightward forces move away from the left lateral leads and write a broad S there.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.197; Khan ch4 p.87–90

cards.q: Name the leads with a broad, notched R wave
cards.a:
I, aVL, V5, V6

The leads over the left ventricle record its slow, late depolarisation as a broad notched R.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.198; Khan ch4 p.99–100

cards.q: Explain: Tell RBBB from LBBB in V1
cards.a: Both are wide, so look at V1. Mostly upward with rSR′ means RBBB. Mostly downward, a deep QS or rS, means LBBB.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.197–198; Khan ch4 p.87, 99

cards.q: In LBBB, the T wave in V6 is usually
cards.a:
Inverted, opposite the R wave

In bundle branch block the ST-T points away from the main QRS deflection.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.199; Khan ch4 p.100

cards.q: rSR′ in V1 with a QRS of 0.11 s is
cards.a:
Incomplete RBBB

The RBBB shape with a QRS between 0.10 and 0.12 s is incomplete RBBB.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.210; Khan ch4 p.93, 99

cards.q:
Deep S waves in V1 with LBBB can be used to diagnose LVH.
True or false?
cards.a: False. LBBB deranges the vectors, so LVH voltage criteria do not apply.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.202; Khan ch4 p.100–105

cards.q: Which bundle branch block makes the ECG diagnosis of infarction most difficult?
cards.a:
LBBB

LBBB distorts the QRS, ST and T of the left ventricle, where most infarcts occur.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.276; Khan ch4 p.100–105

cards.q:
A 64-year-old with chest pain has an LBBB not seen on last year’s ECG. Treat it as urgently as a STEMI.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Thaler: a new LBBB may signify infarction and needs the same urgent attention as a STEMI.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.200, ch6 p.276; Khan ch4 p.106

topics.name: Hemiblocks
topics.desc: Read fascicular blocks from the axis, alone or with RBBB.

cards.q: A hemiblock is a block of
cards.a:
One fascicle of the left bundle

Only the left bundle has fascicles, so hemiblocks are left-sided.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.202–203; Khan ch9 p.216

cards.q: In LAFB, the QRS in II, III and aVF is mainly
cards.a:
Negative (rS)

The main forces run upward, away from the inferior leads, writing deep S waves.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.203; Khan ch9 p.216–218

cards.q: By Thaler’s rule, which finding shows the axis is beyond −30°?
cards.a:
Lead II negative

Lead II sits at +60°; a negative QRS there puts the axis more negative than −30°.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.203–204; Khan ch9 p.217–218

cards.q:
LAFB widens the QRS beyond 0.12 s.
True or false?
cards.a: False. The other fascicles conduct normally, so ventricular depolarisation is not delayed.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.205; Khan ch9 p.218

cards.q: Axis −60°, QRS 0.09 s, otherwise normal ECG. Most likely
cards.a:
LAFB

Narrow QRS, marked left axis and no other cause: left anterior hemiblock.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.204–205

cards.q: LPFB shifts the axis to
cards.a:
Right, about +120° or more

With the posterior fascicle blocked, activation runs downward and rightward.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.204–205; Khan ch9 p.218–219

cards.q:
Right axis deviation in a patient with severe COPD is diagnostic of LPFB.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Lung disease is itself a cause of right axis deviation, so LPFB cannot be diagnosed.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.204; Khan ch9 p.215, 219

cards.q: QRS 0.14 s, rSR′ in V1, axis −60°. This is
cards.a:
RBBB with LAFB

The rSR′ and width give RBBB; the marked left axis adds left anterior hemiblock.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.207–208; Khan ch9 p.219

cards.q: Put Thaler’s order for reading combined blocks
cards.a:
P–QRS relationship: is there AV block? → V1–V6: is there bundle branch block? → Axis: is there a hemiblock?

Work from the top of the conduction system down: AV node, bundles, fascicles.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.211–212

cards.q: During an acute MI a patient suddenly develops AV block plus a new bundle branch block. Thaler’s advice
cards.a:
Pacing, usually temporary

This combination in acute MI warrants a pacemaker, usually removed once the acute event settles.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.212; Khan ch9 p.219

topics.name: Preexcitation
topics.desc: Find the delta wave and know why WPW matters.

cards.q: An accessory pathway lets the impulse
cards.a:
Bypass the AV node delay

The pathway is a short circuit from atrium to ventricle that skips the AV node.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.222–223

cards.q: Explain: WPW sign 1: PR under 0.12 s
cards.a: In Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) ventricular activation starts early, so the PR interval is shorter than 0.12 s: under three small squares.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.224; Khan ch11 p.271

cards.q: Explain: WPW sign 2: the delta wave
cards.a: The early-activated muscle conducts slowly, so the QRS begins with a slurred upstroke: the delta wave. It may show in only some leads, so scan all 12.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.224; Khan ch11 p.271

cards.q: Why is the QRS wide in WPW?
cards.a:
Part of the ventricle is activated early

Unlike bundle branch block, WPW widens the QRS by premature activation.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.224; Khan ch11 p.271

cards.q: In orthodromic AVRT the QRS is
cards.a:
Narrow, as the AV node carries it down

The ventricles are activated through the normal bundle branches, so the QRS is narrow.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.229–231; Khan ch11 p.272–276

cards.q:
An unstable wide-complex tachycardia that might be antidromic AVRT should be treated as VT.
True or false?
cards.a: True. VT is far commoner and can be lethal, so assume VT when you cannot tell.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.230–231; Khan ch11 p.276

cards.q: Irregular, about 260/min, wide complexes of changing shape. Think of
cards.a:
AF conducted down an accessory pathway

Very fast, irregular and bizarre wide beats are the signature of preexcited AF.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.232; Khan ch11 p.276, ch12 p.392

cards.q: Short PR, narrow QRS, no delta wave, and episodes of palpitations. Name it
cards.a:
Lown–Ganong–Levine syndrome

Short PR without a delta wave plus a tachyarrhythmia is Lown–Ganong–Levine syndrome.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.225, 233

cards.q:
A symptomatic accessory pathway can be mapped and ablated at electrophysiology study.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Mapping and ablation is routine for symptomatic WPW and resolves the problem.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.227, 232–233

cards.q: Inferior Q-like waves with a PR of 0.10 s. Before calling an old inferior MI, consider
cards.a:
WPW pseudoinfarct pattern

Negative delta waves mimic Q waves; the short PR gives WPW away.
cards.note: Thaler ch5 p.234, ch6 p.276; Khan ch11 p.271–272

topics.name: Atrial enlargement
topics.desc: Read lead II and V1 for right and left atrial enlargement.

cards.q: The second half of the P wave reflects
cards.a:
The left atrium

The impulse starts in the right atrium near the sinus node and reaches the left atrium last.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.98–99; Khan ch3 p.81

cards.q: Why is the P wave in V1 useful?
cards.a:
It is biphasic, separating right and left atria

V1 lies perpendicular to atrial current, splitting the P into right and left parts.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.99–100

cards.q: The P-wave height in lead II that defines right atrial enlargement
cards.a:
2.5 mm

Both books use 2.5 mm in the inferior leads.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.100–101; Khan ch7 p.181

cards.q: A peaked 3 mm P wave in lead II most suggests
cards.a:
Chronic lung disease

Right atrial enlargement is classically caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.101; Khan ch3 p.83, ch7 p.182–184

cards.q:
A 2 mm positive first half of the P wave in V1 suggests right atrial enlargement.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Khan: an initial positive P component of 1.5 mm or more in V1–V2 indicates right atrial enlargement.
cards.note: Khan ch7 p.181

cards.q: Explain: Left atrial enlargement: broad, notched P
cards.a: In left atrial enlargement the left-atrial part lasts longer, so the P widens to 0.12 s or more in lead II. It is often notched, with peaks more than 0.04 s apart.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.101–102; Khan ch3 p.82, ch7 p.179

cards.q: The terminal negative P in V1 suggests LAE when it is
cards.a:
At least 1 mm deep and 0.04 s wide

One small square deep by one small square wide is the threshold in both books.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.101–102; Khan ch7 p.179

cards.q: Which is a classic cause of P mitrale?
cards.a:
Mitral stenosis

Mitral valve disease loads the left atrium, which then enlarges.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.102; Khan ch7 p.181

cards.q:
P mitrale always means the left atrium is dilated on echo.
True or false?
cards.a: False. ECG atrial changes can occur without enlargement, from pressure, volume or conduction changes.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.95, 102; Khan ch7 p.180–181

topics.name: Ventricular hypertrophy
topics.desc: Apply voltage criteria for LVH and RVH, and know their limits.

cards.q: The key ECG change of ventricular hypertrophy is
cards.a:
Increased QRS amplitude

Hypertrophy criteria are built on increased voltage; the QRS rarely exceeds 0.10 s.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.77–79, 110

cards.q: S in V1 is 14 mm and R in V5 is 18 mm. Sokolow–Lyon is
cards.a:
Not met: 32 mm is not over 35

14 + 18 = 32 mm, which does not exceed 35 mm.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.107–108; Khan ch7 p.185

cards.q:
An R wave of 13 mm in aVL meets a limb-lead criterion for LVH.
True or false?
cards.a: True. R in aVL over 11 mm is a voltage criterion in both books.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.109; Khan ch7 p.185

cards.q: A woman has R in aVL 9 mm and S in V3 13 mm. Cornell is
cards.a:
Met: 22 mm exceeds 20 in women

The threshold is 20 mm for women; 9 + 13 = 22 mm.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.109; Khan ch7 p.185

cards.q: Voltage criterion met plus left axis, nothing else. Romhilt–Estes gives
cards.a:
5 points: LVH

Voltage 3 plus left axis 2 makes 5, which indicates LVH.
cards.note: Khan ch7 p.187

cards.q: Name the leads with strain-type ST depression
cards.a:
I, aVL, V5, V6

Repolarisation changes appear in the leads with the tallest R waves, over the left ventricle.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.111–113; Khan ch7 p.184

cards.q: A hypertensive patient has a normal ECG. This
cards.a:
Does not rule out LVH

The ECG misses about half of echo-proven LVH: sensitivity is low.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.108, 114; Khan ch7 p.184, 187

cards.q: Explain: RVH: R bigger than S in V1
cards.a: In right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) the right ventricle dominates the chest leads. V1 shows an R wave larger than its S, while V6 shows an S larger than its R.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.104–106; Khan ch7 p.187

cards.q: Which finding most supports RVH?
cards.a:
Right axis deviation

A dominant right ventricle pulls the mean QRS axis to the right.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.104–106; Khan ch7 p.187–191

cards.q:
In biventricular hypertrophy the right ventricular signs usually dominate the ECG.
True or false?
cards.a: False. The normally dominant left ventricle usually obscures the right ventricular features.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.110

topics.name: Pacemakers
topics.desc: Recognise paced beats, the mode code and the common failures.

cards.q: Explain: A pacemaker writes a spike
cards.a: A pacemaker is a battery and microchip under the skin, with leads in the right atrium and/or right ventricle. Each time it fires, it writes a sharp, narrow vertical spike.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.212–214; Khan ch10 p.239

cards.q: Demand pacemaker set at 60/min; sinus rhythm at 80/min. You expect
cards.a:
No pacing spikes

The device is inhibited while the native rate is above its set rate.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.213; Khan ch10 p.239

cards.q: A right-ventricular paced QRS resembles
cards.a:
LBBB

Right ventricle first, left ventricle late: the same sequence as left bundle branch block.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.214; Khan ch10 p.239–241

cards.q: Two spikes per beat: one before the P, one before a wide QRS. The pacemaker is
cards.a:
Dual-chamber

It paces the atrium, then the ventricle after a set AV interval.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.214–215; Khan ch10 p.239–243

cards.q: Match each mode
cards.a:
VVI: Ventricular pacing, inhibited by a sensed QRS
AAI: Atrial pacing, inhibited by a sensed P wave
DDD: Paces and senses atrium and ventricle
DOO: Fixed-rate pacing of both chambers

The letters read: chamber paced, chamber sensed, response (I inhibited, D dual, O none).
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.239

cards.q: Pacing spikes appear on time but none is followed by a QRS. This is
cards.a:
Failure to capture

The device fires, but the myocardium is not depolarised.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.219–220; Khan ch10 p.243–245

cards.q:
A spike falling just after a native QRS suggests the pacemaker failed to sense that beat.
True or false?
cards.a: True. A sensing pacemaker would have been inhibited by the native QRS.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.243–244

cards.q: What does an ICD do when it detects VT?
cards.a:
Rapid pacing or a shock

An ICD treats life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias with overdrive pacing or a shock.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.172–173

cards.q: CRT benefits most a patient with poor LV function and
cards.a:
A wide QRS such as LBBB

CRT corrects the dyssynchrony that a wide QRS, especially LBBB, produces.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.216; Khan ch10 p.239

cards.q:
If you cannot see pacing spikes, a pacemaker is ruled out.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Spikes can be tiny; wide QRS with left axis should still prompt you to look for a device.
cards.note: Thaler ch4 p.217
